title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 114 (Ordinary and special resolutions)

content.overview: Section 114 distinguishes ordinary resolutions from special resolutions by both notice and voting requirements.
content.glance: Ordinary: valid votes in favour exceed votes against. Special: notice must specify the intention and votes in favour must be at least three times votes against.
content.study:
## Statutory framework

Section 114 of the Companies Act, 2013 sets the voting test for ordinary and special resolutions. Read it with the meeting-notice requirements in section 101, explanatory statements under section 102 where applicable, and filing duties under section 117.

## Ordinary resolution — section 114(1)

The notice required by the Act must have been duly given. Votes in favour must exceed votes against among members entitled to vote and voting. Do not calculate the majority from the total number of members on the register.

## Special resolution — section 114(2)

The notice or other intimation given to members must specify the intention to propose the resolution as a special resolution; the notice required by the Act must be duly given; and votes in favour must be not less than three times the votes against. These conditions are cumulative. A strong vote cannot cure a defective notice.

## Worked example

100 valid votes for and 40 against meets the ordinary voting test but not the special-resolution ratio. 120 votes for and 40 against meets the 3:1 ratio exactly, provided the notice requirements and all other statutory requirements are satisfied.

## Exam checklist

Identify the resolution and enabling provision; check notice and any explanatory statement; identify valid votes for and against; apply the correct threshold; and check whether section 117 filing is required.

sections.title: Ordinary resolution — s. 114(1)
content: The notice required by the Act must be duly given and valid votes in favour must exceed votes against among members entitled to vote and voting.
The comparison is between votes cast for and against, not the total number of members on the register.

sections.title: Special resolution — s. 114(2)
content: The notice or other intimation must specify the intention to propose the resolution as a special resolution.
Votes in favour must be at least three times votes against, in addition to compliance with the notice requirements.
A numerical majority cannot cure a missing special-resolution notice statement.

cases.name: Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd.
cases.facts: A properly incorporated company was challenged as indistinct from its controlling shareholder.
cases.issue: What is the legal effect of incorporation?
cases.ratioDecidendi: A registered company is a legal person separate from its members, even when control and ownership are concentrated.
cases.holding: The company's separate personality was affirmed.
cases.relevance: Use for Companies Act s. 9 and corporate personality.

cases.name: Foss v. Harbottle
cases.facts: Shareholders sought relief for alleged wrongs to the company.
cases.issue: Who may sue for a wrong done to the company and when may exceptions apply?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The company is the proper plaintiff for corporate wrongs, subject to recognised exceptions such as fraud on the minority and ultra vires acts.
cases.holding: The proper-plaintiff and majority-rule principles were established.
cases.relevance: Use with oppression, mismanagement and class-action analysis.

cases.name: Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court examined share issue powers and alleged oppression.
cases.issue: When does a corporate action become oppressive or invalid?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examines purpose, fairness, statutory power and resulting prejudice rather than treating every irregularity as oppression.
cases.holding: The corporate action was assessed under the statutory and equitable framework.
cases.relevance: Use for share allotment and oppression claims.

cases.name: Miheer H. Mafatlal v. Mafatlal Industries Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court reviewed a scheme of arrangement sanctioned by the company court.
cases.issue: What is the court's role in sanctioning a corporate scheme?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The court must ensure statutory compliance, class fairness, informed approval and absence of illegality, but does not substitute its commercial judgment for the company's decision.
cases.holding: The principles governing scheme sanction were stated.
cases.relevance: Use for corporate arrangements and tribunal scrutiny.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Distinguish ordinary and special resolutions under section 114.
questionsAndAnswers.answer: An ordinary resolution requires valid votes in favour to exceed votes against among members entitled to vote and voting, after due notice. A special resolution additionally requires that the notice or other intimation specify the intention to propose it as a special resolution and that votes in favour are at least three times votes against. The notice and voting tests are cumulative.

examTips: State both the notice and voting tests for a special resolution.
Use a numerical example and distinguish votes cast from total membership.
revisionPoints: Ordinary: votes in favour exceed votes against.
Special: intention stated in notice and votes in favour are at least three times votes against.
Notice compliance and voting threshold are cumulative.
